utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, and are we already linked with the videolink? Yes, we are. And in -- it is Belgrade, isn't it? So good morning to you in Belgrade as well. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; legal intern, Victoria More, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like the record to reflect that the late start is due to technical problems. And then we can start with the new witness. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I take it you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us your name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I stand up? My name is Milosav Djordjevic, and my father's name was Cvetko. I was born on the 27th August, 1935, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so, you commit yourself to -- you expose yourself - sorry - to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to this Tribunal. May I now ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Djordjevic. Can I first ask if --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- you can -- can you see me, hear me, and understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor. I can see you, I can hear you, and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very good. Let me first ask that the Registrar show you the document 65 ter 6393, which is found at tab 19. And I might suggest that it would be more efficient to take this one out of the binder and just place it in front of the witness. He might be referring to it throughout his testimony. General, now do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do. And I also recognise my signature and your initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Is this a witness statement that you provided to members of the Office of the Prosecutor, including myself, in March of this year?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the statement that I provided on the 19th of March, 2013, as the statement that I provided here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, before you signed the statement, were you given an opportunity to read the statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to read the statement in my own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after you signed the statement in the -- in the time that you followed, did you have an opportunity to again review the statement before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on the 2nd of July, I read the statement once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to go over the statement again with me by telephone on Monday of this week, the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during our --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- discussion -- and when we spoke on Monday, then, did you identify some parts of the statement that you would like to make some modifications or -- or clarifications too?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that occasion. And Mr. Stringer, with the help of an interpreter, noted all those things that I mentioned with regard to those pages. I have my own example that you sent to me earlier. I have it on me today, and with your permission I would like to put it on the desk in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine. You can refer to that if you need to, but, General, let me first ask you a couple of questions. I'll take you to what I think are the relevant parts of the statement. Could I ask you to first turn to paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Links between the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, the JNA General Staff, and the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous Provinces from the second half of October to the second half of December 1991 and possible causes so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now about halfway through paragraph 2 there's a reference to the constitution of the SFRY from -- excuse me, 1974. And it was my understanding, General, that you wanted to add that the reference there to the constitution, the specific reference you want to make, is to Article 240 of the constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct you to paragraph 4, which I believe was the next citation that you wanted to add. Do you have paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. The Presidency of the SFRY was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the SFRY, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if I noted it correctly, General, then, you wished to add that the reference to the SFRY constitution here is to Article 316, and that the reference to the Law on All People's Defence is to Article 108 of that law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in the following paragraph, paragraph 5, did you also wish to note that this should refer or mention Article 80 of the Law on All People's Defence in support of this passage?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Law on All People's Defence of Yugoslavia dating back to 1982, which was then in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for the record, General Djordjevic, can you tell us what the specific article of that law that you wanted to supply the citation for here, in paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to refer to the margins of the previous document that I had? Because I made some notes in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't find it, but I believe that things are just the way you put them, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, the reference that I had mentioned was to Article 80 of the Law on All People's Defence. And if we have an opportunity, we can try to come back to that. Does that sound about right, Article 80.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that article, as far as I can remember, there's a reference to the competencies of the Supreme Command, the functioning of the staff of the Supreme Command, i.e., the Presidency, the Ministry of Defence, and the General Staff. The ministry and the General Staff constituted the staff of the Supreme Command, and the Presidency itself is the Supreme Command. I believe that this is what this article is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General, the following paragraph, paragraph 6, I had noted that you wished to add a reference here to Article 97 of the Law on All People's Defence ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- I suppose Belgrade doesn't hear us anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm told the weather is interfering. Shall we wait for the sunshine?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If it's ... may I say something or do I need to wait until Belgrade is back on? It's actually better if I say it outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the conditions, I would respectfully propose, with the Court's permission and perhaps the agreement of my learned friend, to continue leading a little bit just to speed along these additions. I can ask the witness to refer to the notes he made in the margin, but it might slow us down a little bit, which seems a bit risky today, but I did want you to know that I'm aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Belgrade is back, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Heard you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, yes. Are you able to see and hear me again?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I can hear you and I can see you. Can I just ask you something. In paragraph 6, it's not Article 80 of the law but Article 97 of the law where there is a reference to the Territorial Defence as being directly subordinated to the republic. So it is Article 97 of the Law on National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the note I had. And just to clarify now, I believe that it was for paragraph 5 that the reference was to Article 80 of the Law on All People's Defence. Is that also correct, Article 80, for paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely correct. It is Article 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then it's Article 97 for paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in the following paragraph, paragraph 7, you wanted to change the word that currently appears, the word "occupied," and to replace it with some other words instead. Could I ask you just to explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia or the SFRY, dating back to 1974, and based on the Law on All People's Defence dating back to 1982, the term "occupation" does not exist to represent a certain situation during war time. That term is not used. Rather, the term "temporarily taken territory" is used rather than occupation, so I would use that. I would use the word "taken" and that means that the territory is temporarily taken or in the possession of an enemy side or the opposition side. If I may add to that, the explanation was this. If we were to adopt the word "occupation" that would also mean that the enemy side also holds power of that territory and that the result would be a capitulation of that territory. That's why the word "occupation" has been replaced by the temporarily taken territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for that modification. Now, if I understand the next modification, you wanted to add a reference in paragraph 9. So if could you turn to paragraph 9. And this paragraph refers to political factors which triggered the armed conflicts. And, General, if I noted correctly you wanted to add a reference here to the Serb referendum that was held in Croatia on the 2nd of August, 1990, regarding autonomy or unification of municipalities in Croatia with a majority Serb population. And then also the second referendum of Serbs in Croatia on establishing the SAOs after their status was changed in the constitution. Is that a correct description of the additions that you wanted to make in paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, Mr. Prosecutor, I wanted to add that there were two referendums for the Serbs in those areas. In the first case, the intention was to create an autonomy within the framework of the Republic of Croatia; a Serb autonomy in Croatia. When the new constitution was adopted in Croatia, and when it was decided that Croatia would secede from Yugoslavia, then the Serbs made a decision at a referendum to establish their own assembly and that they should also secede from Croatia but to still be -- be an integral part of Yugoslavia. That would be my shortest possible explanation with regard to your question, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now the next modification was in paragraph 10 of your statement. And now this is where you listed some of the possible causes of the crisis and the outcome. And if I noted it correctly, here you wanted to add a reference to statements of leading politicians, such as President Tudjman who had indicated that the NDH was not a nationalist Fascist state but reflected the will of the people, and also President Milosevic who stated that one could not rule out the possibility that differences about Yugoslavia might be resolved by military means. Have I noted that correctly; and would you care to comment on that if I have not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Stringer, Dr. Tudjman made that statement at the Assembly of the so-called Croatian Democratic Union which was a newly established party; whereas, Mr. Milosevic made that statement of his at Gazi Mestan [phoen] where a monument is for the fallen Serbs during the conflict with the Ottoman empire in 1389, where there was a huge rally where almost a million people gathered and the presidency of the SFRY was present. He stated then we are in the midst of battles again. He meant political struggle where Yugoslavia was being put into question and the system in power until then. We are again in political fights. They are not armed fights, but I don't rule that out either. This was an opportunity for other people to interpret that as -- as an announcement of future armed conflict. This is what I had to say, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And now the next modification, I believe, was in paragraph 12, and you wanted to add a reference to three locations that were -- you thought were relevant to this. Can you describe those or mention those to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the early spring - I believe it was March 1991 - the first clashes happened in Croatia between the self-organised Serbs and the special forces of the Croatian MUP. It was by the Plitvice lakes. They are well-known for their beauty. The next clash was at Borovo Selo in the month of May when there was shooting too, when Croatian police, as far as I was able to learn in the meantime but back then I didn't know, they killed a number of civilians, and then there was the Bakrac case which is a small town in Slavonia east of Zagreb where there was also shooting, and that was also in May 1991. Then the Presidency of the SFRY sent some of their members, among them Mr. Stjepan Mesic, who I was a new -- a recent arrival at the Presidency. They sent their members there to a fact-finding mission. I don't want to go into all the details, among others, because I don't know them all, and it was decided that JNA units in Croatia where there were clashes between Croats and Serbs - conditionally speaking, though it would be better to say between paramilitaries of both sides - that JNA units should be there as a buffer to prevent further clashes until the burning issues were resolved politically. This is it, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I've noted that the next addition you wanted to make in -- is in paragraph 13 regarding military factors. And, here, you wanted to add a reference to a book published by Croatian General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right, on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe that you have referred to this book in another part of your statement but you wanted to add a reference to it here as well. Can you briefly describe for the Judges what you wanted to add to your statement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe we've lost it again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, are you --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, could you then briefly tell us what it was that you read in General Spegelj's book that you wanted to refer to here in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I must point out, Mr. Prosecutor, that in 1991 I did not have that information. I learned it by reading Mr. Spegelj's book. He was a minister of defence. He was chief of General Staff and in other high positions. And the title of the book is "The Memories of a Soldier." It was published in Zagreb. He says there that the Yugoslav People's Army in the 5th Military District, which is mostly Croatia and Slovenia, including Bihac, a town in western Bosnia. These are the territories of the 5th Military District. That the JNA then had 44.000 men of a total of 160- or 170.000 that the JNA had in all. Of those 44.000, 26 per cent were Serbs and Montenegrins; 22 per cent were Croats; 8 per cent Muslims; 7 per cent Slovenians; 4 per cent Macedonians; and 4 per cent Hungarians, Ruthenians, Slovaks, and others. I believe that this is important information because in the language used from the 1990s there's a mention of the aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army against Croatia. I object to that term. How can this joint military force of the still-existing countries be an aggressor in its own country? This is my conclusion from the precise information that General Spegelj published in his book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was there anything else on paragraph 13, or should we move to the next?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we can move on. Thanks. There's nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 15, I think you wanted to indicate that, in regard to the lack of response to the mobilisation, or the call-up, that some 17.000 did not respond to the call-up. Did I note that correctly, for paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, that's correct. We're talking about 17.000 conscripts who were duty-bound to respond to the call-up. In Slovenia, in the summer of 1991, hardly anyone responded. And Croatia was second in that respect. Followed by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and so on. I'm speaking of a total of 17.000 conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 22, General, where you're referring to a number of incidents that occurred in Croatia in attacks or --or activities related to the JNA, that you wanted to add, again, a reference to something you'd read in General Spegelj's book.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. General Spegelj states that from mid-September - or, more precisely, the 13th of September, 1991 - until the 20th of December of the same year, the Croatian army, according to him, came by some weapons; that is, through fighting and attacks on the JNA barracks, and these weapons were taken. And then he goes on to list 200.000 pieces of infantry weapons; 450 mortars and recoilless guns; 180 artillery pieces, he also goes into detail as regards the calibre and so on; 280 cutting-edge anti-armour missiles, mostly mounted to vehicles but not exclusively. Then 500 portable -- or, I'm sorry, 50 pieces of portable anti-aircraft missiles; 130 anti-aircraft guns; 380 missile launchers of the anti-aircraft defence for low altitudes, specifically I'm referring to the Strela 2M model. And my question to the interpreters: Am I speaking too fast?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of tanks; 320 armoured personnel carriers; 500.000 tonnes of ammunition, 500.000 tonnes; 1700 tonnes of explosives; 800 radios; 30 radars; 500 tonnes of anti-aircraft --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of anti-personnel mines; 2.000 vehicles, motor vehicles. And finally, on page 290 of his book, he states that the Croatian armed forces in December 1991 and January 1992 had a numerical strength of about 250.000 armed men belonging to 63 brigades and dozens of battalions. This is what I wanted to add, Mr. Prosecutor, for you to have a better picture of the situation in the latter half of 1992 [as interpreted] in Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to correct the record there possibly. Your -- in your last -- the last sentence you just referred to giving a better picture of the situation in the latter half of 1992. Have you been talking about late 1992 or ... because in the previous paragraph, you mentioned late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I said 1992, I misspoke. I meant the latter half of 1991; from September through December 1991. That's the period General Spegelj discusses in his book, and he gives these figures for that period. And he says that the Croatian armed forces had a total numerical strength of 250.000 armed men and that -- that applies to December 1991 and January 1992. The year 1992 was mentioned in that context only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, I'd like to take you back to paragraph 17 of your statement. I want to show you just a couple of the documents. So if you could turn to paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me first ask you: General, in paragraph 17, do you see about halfway down, that you refer to a series of documents that relate to accepting and regulating volunteers who are coming in to the Serb armed forces, the JNA, or the TOs. Do you see the references to those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the documents --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There's mention of the decree of the government of Serbia dated the 14th of August, 1991, about the registration of volunteers with the Territorial Defence. That is one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. I've got a question for you about that one. And with the Registrar's help, I'm going to ask that he show you the document 65 ter 773.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, what we're doing here is looking to substitute a better copy version of 773 for the one that is technically referred to in his statement. That is to say, 65 ter 773, we're going to try to substitute that now with 773.1 and also what's been marked 773.2, because the copy is better. And also it splits two different laws into two separate documents. And the Defence has been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Looks like I can't proceed quite yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, do we have you again?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you very well. I have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It bears number 743 on the left side, and it's the original version from the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And could I just confirm for the record that -- with the Registrar that the witness is looking at 65 ter 773.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I heard the confirmation from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't -- I didn't hear that. I didn't get that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the document that's in front of you that you've just referred to as Law Number 743, is that the document referring to in paragraph 17 dated 14 August 1991 on the registration of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. This is the document I am speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then with the Registrar's assistance, I'd ask you to look at document 65 ter 773.2.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that is? Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order -- yes, of course, I see it. 773.2. That's the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is in the --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner there is a number 899 in the Serbian original. It's an order of the Presidency of the SFRY on the engagement of volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY during imminent threat of war. It's dated 10 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, the question here is simply to ask you whether you also refer to this law in paragraph 17 of your statement. It's the last of the four documents that we -- you refer to here.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Actually, I'm citing these documents because the paramilitary units that were established more or less voluntarily were to become legal armed forces where volunteers would be accepted under different criteria than party affiliations or ethnicity, and so on. That is what I wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now the last couple of questions I have relate to paragraph 42 of your statement. If I could ask you to turn, please, to paragraph 42. And, General, while you're finding that, just to refresh you, in paragraph 42, you're referring to what you've just described as the -- some of the legislation or steps taken to incorporate volunteers into TO units and to put them under the command of the local TO or JNA, as you say, in paragraph 42. And then you say the issue was addressed by the regulation on enlisting volunteers, issued by the government of Serbia on 23 August 1991. And the English version actually has a typographical error where it includes the number 23 twice. General, my question is this --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I made a mistake. It was not the 23rd but, rather, the 14th of August. We saw the document a minute ago. This should be corrected. So issued by the government of Serbia on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That was -- that was my question. So this is a reference again to the law we just looked at, 773.1, dated 14 August, not 23 August.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And with that, Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders the witness's statement, 65 ter 6393, together with the associated exhibits noting the substitution of 773.1 and 773.2 instead of 65 ter 773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh. You -- did you rise, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to say no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement, 65 ter 6393, receives exhibit number P2300. 65 ter 00773.1 receives exhibit number P2301.2300. And 65 ter 773.2 receives exhibit number P2302.2300. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two additional associated exhibits that are normally marked by the Registrar after the witness is finished testifying. I can note those for the record but they're noted on the spreadsheet that's been distributed. They are 65 ter 297 and 405. Those are also referred to in paragraph 17 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall we give them numbers immediately Madam Registrar or wait for a memo? I think it's -- they're only two so we can do it immediately. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, 65 ter 297 will be Exhibit P2303.2300. And 65 ter 405 will be Exhibit P2304.2300. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for cross, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I start my cross, I would -- I noticed that the Prosecution did not ask the -- two questions to the witness as to Rule 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for that. It was -- I got a bit -- too far down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General Djordjevic, I do have one last question. Now that we've discussed all of the modifications, the additions that you had raised when we spoke on Monday, do you affirm the truthfulness and the accuracy of the statement that is in front of you, taking into account the corrections that you've just made?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I confirm that this is my statement and that it reflects my words faithfully, and we have just made the necessary corrections to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if -- if we were to ask you questions about all of these same issues again today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, Mr. Prosecutor, my answers would be the same, if this were to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can tender it again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- if it's necessary. I appreciate counsel's pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think it's okay, Mr. Stringer. We have it on the record. Even if it is before these or more sacral statement. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Zivanovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Back in business, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's disconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear us, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we hear each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Djordjevic, first of all, I'd like to ask you the following. In your statement, you pointed out, you said, you said that you were in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia between mid-October until the 20th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that you were involved in work that had to do with links with the SAO Krajina, that you were in this co-ordination group that basically contacted the SAO Krajina. Was my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: With the SAO Krajinas, Mr. Zivanovic. I mean, all three SAOs, although the focus was on the so-called Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 66 of your statement, we can take a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that appointments -- you said, inter alia, that the order for the establishment of the co-ordination group of the Serbian Ministry of Defence was issued by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and that the personnel administration of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence was in charge of appointing officers who were to be employed in the republic's administration. This is what I would be interested in now. I actually understand this part of the statement but I'm just asking whether that also pertained to other employees in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, Mr. Zivanovic, the Federal Secretariat for national Defence, by way of its orders, appoints officers from the rank of colonel downwards in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia as permanent employees in that ministry of the republic; whereas, the Presidency of the SFRY appoints generals in the Ministry of Defence or, rather, makes them available to the government and Assembly of the Republic of Serbia that then appoints them at a session of the assembly on the basis of an order issued by the Presidency. That they are being transferred to the republic, but it is the republic that appoints them specifically in the ministry and we, the co-ordination group, we are just there as a temporary single organ on the basis of the order of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. Because we were about to retire or had just retired. We did not have a regular assignment in units, commands, institutions of the JNA, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 67 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- it says that: "The personnel administration and the General Staff Mobilisation Administration sent a group of retired JNA officers, or officers pending retirement, to be attached to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia on a temporary basis." Later on, it says that the ministry deployed some of its ministers -- some of its officers in the newly appointed units or military territorial organs, VTO, which units were responsible for recruiting and mobilisation. Could you clarify that a bit?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I would, Counsel, Mr. Zivanovic. This is what it is all about: Up until then, the Autumn of 1991, the Autumn of 1991, mobilisation was carried out by the Ministry of Defence of the republics through its secretariats of defence, in cities, in municipalities, and so on. However, the Presidency decided that this task should be taken from the Ministry of Defence and that it should be transferred to the so-called military departments. Military territorial organs, rather, that were territorial organs of the JNA, that they should deal with recruitment and mobilisation. Since this was a transition period, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia sent a certain number of officers to these newly appointed territorial organs. I cannot say exactly how many. However, they did not have the necessary number of officers, so then in agreement with the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, they agreed that this co-ordination group for the SAO Krajina should be established, and I was a member of that group. That was it, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of your statement, that is, paragraph 68 --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- you say that this group mediated between the Territorial Defence Staff of the SAO Krajina and the logistics sector of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and the agencies of the 1st Army District Command for issuing necessary supplies and materials.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, for various supplies for the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina, its organs had to turn to the organs of the Republic of Serbia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it was just a mediator, an intermediary, vis-a-vis the 1st Army District and this logistic centre of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. May I just provide a brief explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Staffs sent -- commanders of staffs from the Krajina sent their requests to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, and sometimes these requested would be sent to us too. Although we were not, de jure, the organ that was supposed to do this. We were just there as an intermediary, and then these requests would be examined in these two institutions: The command of the 1st Military District and the logistics administrations of the Federal Secretariat. And then on the basis of that, a decision would be made on the quantities that would be made available to them. However, we did not drive that out, if I may put it that way, sorry. This was done by these JNA institutions that I already referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you documents that have to do with the involvement of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is, 297, dated 13th of September, 1991. Could we please take a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an instruction from the 3rd Administration of the General Staff but it bears the signature of General Kadijevic, the federal secretary of national defence. And 3rd Administration was otherwise in charge of organisation, establishment, and mobilisation. Mobilisation -- I mean, the recruitment system, if I can put it that way, and mobilising reserves and so on and so forth, volunteers, et cetera. In a word, mobilisation of the human potential of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at this document, 297.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at this text, I think it is quite clear that we see how volunteers are admitted into the Yugoslav People's Army. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Zivanovic. There should have been an attachment here, a statement, you see, for the admission of volunteers into the JNA and TO. This was a standard form, including personal and details and so on. However, it's not indispensable. It goes without saying that that should be attached to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second document that was shown to you by the Prosecution, 773.2, that also regulates admission into the JNA of volunteers. The 10th of December is the date. So it's three months later.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the reason why it is necessary to publish two documents for the -- absolutely same thing? The first document had resolved everything.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it happened that way because of the increasing number of objections in the public and among the authorities, including the organs of the Republic of Serbia, in relation to the behaviour of the volunteers. And the fact that they were being admitted without applying criteria that were indispensable for admission into the JNA and Territorial Defence. So this was supposed to be dealt with at the highest level possible. And it should be made binding on the subordinates and everybody is subordinate to the Supreme Command of the JNA. Everybody strictly, therefore, had to apply these orders and instructions that had been issued even in the previous period. However, this could have been done at one particular point in time but I don't know whether it's a question of co-ordination or whatever. But, anyway, there are three documents regulating one and the seam issue. I don't have a convincing answer except for providing this personal point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, do you believe that that first document that I showed you, the -- dated 13th of September, 1991, was it consistently applied?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It had to be applied. Now whether it was applied, Mr. Zivanovic, in practice, that I cannot confirm for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at paragraph 7 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That we're talking about. This order envisages that volunteer formations that are engaged outside the armed forces of the SFRY and that are carrying out certain tasks have to be placed either under the command of the armed forces of the SFRY, in accordance with regulations and this order, within ten days.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was also stated that if they are not involved in the armed forces in the manner prescribed, they would be removed from the territory.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Outside the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Outside the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I would be interested in now: Why -- do you know know, actually, why this was not applied up until the 10th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think -- this is my feeling. This is just my very own thought. A large number of people, Serbia included, that the JNA and the Territorial Defence relied on then, actually, not the Krajina, but Serbia, were trying to dodge the draft and many fled abroad. And probably it is for that reason, namely, there weren't enough soldiers, if I can put it that way, in the Territorial Defence units, first and foremost, but also JNA. This was tacitly accepted, that part of these volunteers that had already been involved were taken in; that is to say, the Territorial Defence of one or the other Krajina and so on. And in order to bring all of this into accord with legal regulations, that is why this was prescribed that way. Also, certain sanctions would be imposed on those who did not abide by that because at first the volunteers did not wish to be under the jurisdiction of JNA commands or under the command of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina that already become official by that point in time. Or perhaps if they were placed under their command, they did it gingerly if I can put it that way. So I don't know if that's an answer that satisfies you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you explain why these people were simply not mobilised into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic when this so-called courier comes, the person who bringing call-up papers, many would say, "He's absent." "We don't know where he is." "He's away on a trip," and so on. Quite simply, they didn't want to go. Now, this is my very own point of view as a citizen. Many did not believe in the final outcome of all of these conflicts and they didn't know what it was that they were supposed to be fighting for. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. If they were not mobilised at their homes, they could have been mobilised once they were in a volunteer unit on the spot, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, those who were already in volunteer units had to be placed under the command either of the Territorial Defence or the JNA, and there was need -- no need for them to be called up again and recruited, quite simply, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me roughly when it was that they were placed under the command of the JNA or, rather, the Territorial Defence, as you say?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in early October 1991, after this government order, after all these interventions. Even we from the co-ordination group drafted a report based on the information received from the staffs of the Krajinas, and Minister Simovic forwarded that report to the General Staff upon which General Adzic demanded that this be strictly implemented, as well as the instruction that was to follow from the federal secretary and the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do tell me if, as far as you know, the Ministry of Defence had contacts with these volunteers' formations.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the Ministry of Defence, in principle, had no correspondence with volunteers. They didn't discuss anything with them. However, there were individual meetings. Now, of course, I cannot remember at each individual meeting who met whom. But there was something irregular, and I'll tell you what. The head of office of the then-Ministry of Defence, General Simovic, Dobrila Gajic-Glisic, in his statement given to this same name Tribunal, mentions that thousands of volunteers of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and so on, of which not one word is true. At least not while I was at the Ministry of Defence. The Ministry of Defence of Serbia or my co-ordination group did not deploy volunteers. We only dealt with officers who were to assigned to the TO Staff of Knin or Pakrac or Beli Manastir, to Mr. Hadzic's staff, or -- or what have you, but we had nothing to do with the volunteers. It was the -- it was the military departments that dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned staffs, which staff did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, the staff of the Territorial Defence. But, unfortunately, I didn't know the commander or the person in charge, so I couldn't give you the name or their rank. Some of my officers were in communication with the people from the TO Staff of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. They exchanged some information and so on, but not me. So I'm not familiar with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that you said that you know the statement of Dobrila Gajic-Glisic. In her statement, as far as I know, she mentioned one Kojic, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now you've reminded me but I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any communication between the Ministry of Defence and this man who, for a while, was a TO commander in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have no information whatsoever about that. But if I may, once there was a volunteers' leader, the leader of some volunteer soldiers. He came to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia. I know that that man was a first-day partisan in the Second World War, and General Simovic told me to receive him to hear what he wanted. If I may continue. This leader of that group of volunteers asked us to provide five buses. And I asked him, "But where are you going? Who are you going to? Under whose command will you place yourself?" And he replied to me -- I believe that he hailed from those areas. He said, "Over there," or "yonder." And I replied, "Dear sir, contact those who promised that to you. We don't recruit volunteers and we don't provide buses." This is all I remember, but anything else as concerns Mr. Kojic and General Simovic isn't anything I can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll now show you a document that was drafted before you -- before your time at the Ministry of Defence, but it may jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 1D501.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 18th of September, 1991. You can see that it was -- it originated from the Ministry of Defence and was sent to Martic and Kojic. And it mentions the Territorial Defences of the SAO Krajina, the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and that this is an order. And a complete cease-fire is to be established as of the 18th of September, 1991, and so on. We can turn the page now.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, I can see it, cease-fire, it says. Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me finish. You can see that the signatory is General Simovic, minister.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this before. I didn't know about this document then, nor do I know anything about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the last page of the English version. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it right away, General, that this document was drafted before you took up your job at the Ministry of Defence of Serbia. However, based on this, can I tell that General Simovic issued direct orders to the commander of the TO of Krajina, SAO Krajina, and the commander of the TO of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Now I wanted too ask you if you are familiar with this and if there were such occurrences at your -- during your time at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zivanovic, I've never seen this document before. It is not my intention to justify this because this puts into question my whole statement. But if you read what it says above the words "I hereby order," namely, that President Tudjman and President Milosevic agreed on a cease-fire, and so on, and in connection with that, I hereby order, and so on. But to the extent I knew the constitutional Law on All People's Defence, General Simovic had no right to issue such orders. He was evenly entitled to inform others and give instructions, bear that in mind, take care that, and so on. However, this is an order. This is the way I see it anyway. At my time, I never saw any such orders. Only information documents and -- and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have mentioned the testimony of Dobrila Gajic-Glisic, and you heard that testimony. Did you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, is this a different topic? I'm looking at the time, and it is more or less time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could make a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Appropriate? Thank you. General Djordjevic, we'll take our first break right now. 30 minutes. So we will be back at, let's say, 11.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just for planning purposes, how long do you think your cross-examination will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think not more than 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stringer, is your next witness available or are you able to makes him to be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Mr. President. We'll double-check just in the course of the next few minutes though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document I just used with -- before the break with the witness. It is 1D501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I see you rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We would object to it, Mr. President. The witness said he has never seen it before and that he couldn't make any comment on it. I can -- I was just noting the transcript reference. And I can give that to Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we all remember what he said, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will further ask the witness about some facts from this document, Your Honour, before I definitely ask to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you must have this document we discussed before the break before you. Do tell me if you can recognise the signature of Mr. Simovic on this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it's difficult to make out. It's rather blurred. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the stamp of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The stamp, yes. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We would, again, assert an objection to the admission of the document. Just because it bears the stamp of the Serbian Ministry of Defence doesn't mean it's admissible through this witness who said at page 32, line 2, that he's never seen it before, he didn't know about this document then "nor do I know anything about it now." I think there's simply not enough of a foundation that's been laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard the testimony of Dobrila Gajic-Glisic.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zivanovic, I was not listening to it. I didn't hear it. I took it off the Internet from the web site of the Humanitarian Law Fund. I didn't hear the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. But, at any rate, you are familiar with the content?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Do you want me to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, if you have a general comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That story of hers, for example, that Mr. Raznjatovic came there -- came to the Ministry of Defence with a bloody rifle and that he went there a number of times, I cannot say a word about that because I have no idea. I only meant Mr. Raznjatovic once in my entire life, and when he came with Mr. Hadzic - I don't know in what capacity - and especially I don't know anything about these assertions about bloody rifles and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was any contact between the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan; that is, his Serbian Volunteers Guard?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. Zivanovic, but I cannot say whether or not anybody from the ministry contacted him. But not to my knowledge. The first and last time I saw him he was with Mr. Hadzic. And I know that later on General Simovic entered the office and warned him to remove his colonel's rank because he was wearing one. I'm not sure how he addressed him, by his first name or otherwise, and he told him, "You only have the right to wear a rank when you are promoted to that rank through an order of the federal ministry." And that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes. He said that to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Hadzic and he came for the first time, and when I met them in the office. I know that Mr. Hadzic came to see the minister, but the then-newly appointed minister of foreign affairs of Serbia, Vladislav Jovanovic also came. And General Simovic summoned me to talk to Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic was present. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you said something about that in paragraph 71 of your statement so we can return to that.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you another document, 1D499. The Serbian text is rather pale, but the English translation is clearly visible. It's a very short document, so if you cannot read it, I can read it out to you. Can you read the Serbian text? Can you see it well?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, in parenthesis Arkan's group, and there is an account number, and beneath that a comment stating that each month regularly payments with the assistance of RSNO (Simovic) and signed by Frenki. Let me just finish. And we see the date of 10 December 1991 in the upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before, Mr. Zivanovic. I have no idea what this is about. Nor do I know this man, Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask you about Frenki. Merely tell me whether you know that the Serbian Volunteers Guard was funded with the assistance of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia? At least that's the way I interpret this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Zivanovic. I know that we made a proposal, that the minister processed, and that they turned to the General Staff to regulate the matter of volunteers and reservists. As for Arkan and his men, I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The TO members were paid regularly, I suppose. Not through the mediation of Jugoskandik?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it, Mr. Zivanovic. This company, Jugoskandik, financing these things, never heard of this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a proposal for regular payments to be effected to members of the TO, and my question is whether that all went regularly and legally through the Ministry of Defence or the TO or whichever way, or whether payments went through Jugoskandik as this document suggests?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the first thing about this Skandik or whatever it's called, but I know that in December or maybe in January 1992, the decision was passed for the government of the Serbia and the SSNO to send money to -- I express myself in plain language, to the SDK at Glina, Banja Luka, and Novi Sad from where the monies were distributed on to the financial bodies of the TO staffs for money, for revenue, or income to be dispersed. I don't know anything about Jugoskandik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, payment through the SDK was the regular channels as prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you. And I would just like to us clarify paragraph 71 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- where you say that you were present when Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, came to the Ministry of --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, he brought some paper with a request for 30.000 or 40.000 grenades for a gun, a cannon, that was practically not being used anymore, was dated at any rate. This is what I would be interested in now. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir? Counsel? May I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you heard my entire question because I see that there was an interruption again.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was that Mr. Goran Hadzic was not familiar with the criteria. For example, as far as combat kits are concerned, how many grenades are needed for one gun and so on. Somebody from his staff brought that to him, and I said to him, "Mr. Hadzic, I don't know if all of the JNA has that many grenades." You noticed that very well, Mr. Zivanovic. Some would be found of these guns but they were obsolete. And then when such requests were brought in, then a person took this upon himself, and I asked Mr. Hadzic to send another request to say how many guns they had, and then, on the basis of the valid criteria for the armed forces, then it would be determined how many grenades they would get, and then this colonel would get that through the 1st Military District. I'm not aware of what happened afterwards. This is just an episode, not particularly intriguing or important. So ... that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished my cross-examination. Your Honours, I would just tender this document, 1D499, although I -- I know for the outcome but I must propose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The -- our -- Prosecution objects on the grounds that a foundation has not been laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have -- one -- one very brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- issue for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General Djordjevic, you were just asked a moment ago about this issue of salaries and you referred to a proposal that was made regarding salaries. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to paragraph 39 of your statement, please. And just for the -- the Chamber's information, does this --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- does this paragraph relate to the issue that you just spoke about on the issue of -- or the proposal in respect of salaries?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it is related to that, although I would like to repeat that I don't know about Jugoskandik and the rest. This is correctly stated, and that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as indicated here, then, your proposal had not been implemented as of December when you left the co-ordination office in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until then, it hadn't been implemented, but I heard -- excuse me for a moment. I see that -- I see on the basis of certain papers that they started making these payments from January 1992. Now whether they were making retroactive payments as well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about whether such payments were made after you left the co-ordination group?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't, no. Mr. Stringer, Mr. Prosecutor, the co-ordination group was practically dissolved after I left. A colonel stayed on from that group. I cannot recall his name right now. I heard that he died a few years ago as well. I heard that from another person. He stayed behind to take care of some of the papers there that had remained from our work, and he stayed there to hand over all of that to the Ministry of Defence, and this co-ordination group was never re-established, so I never had any opportunity to contact them or to express any interest in these payments, salaries, and so on. That would be my answer, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Witness, I have a clarification question to ask you with regard to your testimony this morning. On transcript page 29 and 30, so pages 29 and 30, you said that the Ministry of Defence in Serbia did not deal with voluntary -- volunteers, in principle, nor did your co-ordination group. Your co-ordination group was not in charge of deploying volunteers; but, at the same time, you said that the military departments were in charge of them. I'm referring to page 30, line 8: "It was the military departments that dealt with them." So there something I don't understand because it seems that there is a contradiction here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Mindua, I'm going to repeat this in case you haven't noticed. The Ministry of Defence of Serbia, through its secretariats at lower-ranking communities, cities, municipalities, et cetera, they dealt with all of this work until the autumn of 1991, and then all matters related to recruitment, that is to say, call-up into the armed forces, then taking in volunteers, registering them, and deploying them to particular unit, all of this was transferred to the military departments. Military departments are organs that remain in the territory. They are not units that are involved in manoeuvres on the ground. They have military departments in different cities. And I mentioned that the Ministry of Defence, at that point in time, that is to say, during this hand-over stage, if I can put it that way, between the Ministry of Defence and the JNA organ, that is to say, military departments, they sent some military officers to these military departments and then they had less officers in the ministry itself. And then we, as a some kind of temporary organ, appeared there to take care of some of this work. So there is no nothing controversial about it. Quite simply, this transitional period between the Ministry of Defence dealing with this and the armed forces and their organs dealing with it. That is to say, the military territorial organs, the military departments. I hope that that was satisfactory. I'm prepared to give further explanations, if necessary. Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It's very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General Djordjevic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for assisting the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, do you have a next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, we are here with one of our interns, Ms. Khushboo Shahdadpuri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, we can perhaps deal with two oral rulings. The one I started -- I mentioned yesterday with regard to the motion to admit Exhibit 1D468 filed on the 27th of June, pertaining to a videolink, the Defence stated that the Prosecution has no objection, and I asked whether that was correct. Mr. Stringer? Can you -- do you have an answer to that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I have -- if -- if the Defence has -- has indicated that the Prosecution has no objection, I have no reason to question that. I don't -- I don't have in my mind at the moment the specific document involved, but if -- if that is, indeed, the Prosecution position we've expressed to the Defence I'm sure it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It was written on hard copy paper, Mr. Stringer, so -- Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I could perhaps assist. This is a reminder. This is about the Latinica video for which a transcript was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct. There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The motion is granted. The Registry shall mark the video and accompanying transcripts as admitted into evidence. The Defence is reminded that copies of videos and their transcripts must be provided to the Prosecution, Registry, and Chamber in advance of them being tendered as evidence. Second oral ruling is in private session. Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Do you hear me in a language you understand? Mr. Witness, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal, Mr. Witness. May I ask you to state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jozo Knezevic, the 20th -- the 22nd of July, 1960.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have trouble hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, could you speak a little bit louder, please. The interpreters have difficulty hearing you. You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury, should you give untruthful information to the Tribunal. Please read the solemn declaration now the court usher will give you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You already provided the Trial Chamber with your name and your date of birth. Can you tell the Court where you were born?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And where have you been living since you were born until the start of the conflict in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in Tenja, who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: With my parents. My mother, father, and brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, before the beginning of the conflict, what was your profession or your line of work?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked at the factory that manufactured agricultural machinery, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this was in the village of Tenja?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, it Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have any siblings?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I have two brothers and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell the Trial Chamber in which part of Tenja you were living at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The old part of Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And I will show you in a moment an aerial image of Tenja, and I would like you to help us locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 6304, please, at tab 11 of our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, on screen, on the right-hand screen, you will see an image of Tenja. You can just wait for a moment. Yes. Are you -- are you familiar with this picture?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know much about this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe if we can zoom a little bit into the centre of the picture. Do you remember having seen this picture before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, about a month ago, do you remember having been met by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember on that occasion being shown an image of Tenja?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the one that we have on the screen, is this not the image that was shown to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot -- well, I think it is. I don't know. Somehow it's not exactly familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Are you -- you're not able to situate yourself with this image?

utterances.speaker: JOZO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
